title: Fixed deposits
summary: Understand fixed-rate deposits, access restrictions, and the role they can play in shorter-horizon planning.
purpose: Setting aside money for a defined period with a stated interest rate.
riskLabel: Generally lower variability, with institution and inflation considerations
variability: The stated rate is usually fixed for the deposit term, while the real value of the money can change with inflation.
typicalHorizon: Months to several years, depending on the deposit term.
liquidity: Often accessible before maturity with conditions or penalties; exact terms vary.
minimumPracticalAmount: Varies by institution and deposit type.
costs: Review premature-withdrawal conditions, renewal settings, and any linked-account charges.
taxCaveat: Interest and tax treatment depend on current law and personal circumstances; verify before acting.
advantages: Simple structure and a stated rate for a defined term.
Useful for learning how maturity dates can map to planned expenses.
limitations: Early access can change the effective return or trigger a penalty.
commonMistakes: Treating every institution and deposit as identical.
Ignoring maturity instructions and access conditions.

title: Government-backed savings
summary: Learn how different government-backed savings structures vary in eligibility, term, access, and tax treatment.
purpose: Saving toward defined medium- or long-term needs through schemes with government backing.
riskLabel: Lower credit-risk perception does not remove term, access, or inflation trade-offs
variability: Terms may be stated, but rates, contribution rules, and future scheme conditions can change.
typicalHorizon: Often multiple years; each scheme has its own term.
liquidity: Frequently restricted, conditional, or tied to a maturity schedule.
minimumPracticalAmount: Scheme-specific; eligibility and contribution limits can apply.
costs: Review administrative rules, missed-contribution effects, and exit conditions.
taxCaveat: Deductions, exemptions, and maturity treatment vary by scheme and can change.
advantages: Can support disciplined saving for a defined purpose.
Published scheme rules make comparison possible.
limitations: Long lock-ins can conflict with emergency needs.
Eligibility and contribution limits may restrict access.
commonMistakes: Selecting a scheme for a tax feature without checking the term.
Using locked savings as an emergency fund.

title: Bonds
summary: Learn how issuer quality, interest-rate movement, maturity, and market liquidity affect debt instruments.
purpose: Lending money to an issuer in exchange for defined payment obligations.
riskLabel: Ranges widely by issuer, structure, maturity, and market conditions
variability: Market values can move when interest rates or credit expectations change.
typicalHorizon: Commonly matched to a maturity date or a multi-year goal.
liquidity: Some instruments trade actively while others can be difficult to exit.
minimumPracticalAmount: Varies by instrument and access channel.
costs: Consider spreads, platform charges, taxes, and the effect of exiting before maturity.
taxCaveat: Interest and capital treatment depend on instrument structure and current law.
advantages: Introduces defined payment schedules and maturity planning.
Can help explain the difference between credit risk and price variability.
limitations: Issuer default and downgrade risk can cause losses.
A quoted yield is not a guarantee of the realised outcome.
commonMistakes: Looking only at the highest quoted yield.
Assuming every bond is easy to exit.

title: Diversified mutual funds
summary: Understand pooled investing, category differences, diversification, costs, and why fund labels matter.
purpose: Pooling money across a managed basket of assets according to a stated mandate.
riskLabel: Depends on the underlying assets, mandate, concentration, and duration
variability: Values change with the underlying portfolio; different categories can behave very differently.
typicalHorizon: From shorter-term debt-oriented learning to long-term equity-oriented learning.
liquidity: Many open-ended structures offer periodic access, subject to settlement and scheme rules.
minimumPracticalAmount: Varies by scheme and contribution method.
costs: Review expense ratios, exit conditions, taxes, and tracking or management differences.
taxCaveat: Tax treatment differs by portfolio composition, holding period, and current rules.
advantages: Makes diversification and professional management easier to study.
Published mandates provide a basis for category comparison.
limitations: A broad category name can hide important portfolio differences.
Diversification reduces some risks but cannot remove market losses.
commonMistakes: Following recent performance without reading the mandate.
Treating all mutual-fund categories as having the same risk.

title: Equity and stock learning
summary: Study ownership, business quality, diversification, valuation uncertainty, and large market declines without security picks.
purpose: Learning how ownership in businesses can participate in long-term growth while accepting uncertainty.
riskLabel: High variability and a real possibility of substantial or permanent loss
variability: Prices can move sharply and remain below prior levels for long periods.
typicalHorizon: Usually studied in a long-term context rather than for near-term spending needs.
liquidity: Market access does not guarantee a favourable exit price.
minimumPracticalAmount: Learning does not require committing money; market access and lot rules vary.
costs: Consider brokerage, taxes, spreads, research time, and concentration risk.
taxCaveat: Tax treatment depends on transaction type, holding period, and current law.
advantages: Builds understanding of business ownership and compounding.
Makes the cost of concentration and weak analysis visible.
limitations: Company-specific outcomes can differ dramatically from broad markets.
Past performance and a familiar brand do not establish future outcomes.
commonMistakes: Confusing a good company with an attractive valuation.
Concentrating money needed for near-term goals.

title: Gold
summary: Compare physical and financial forms of gold, price variability, storage, liquidity, and concentration.
purpose: Learning how gold can behave differently from income-producing assets.
riskLabel: Market-linked variability with product-form, storage, and concentration considerations
variability: Prices can rise or fall for extended periods and do not produce business earnings.
typicalHorizon: Commonly considered in medium- or long-term diversification discussions.
liquidity: Depends on the form, market, purity verification, and exit channel.
minimumPracticalAmount: Varies widely across physical and financial forms.
costs: Review spreads, making charges, storage, insurance, custody, and product expenses.
taxCaveat: Tax treatment depends on the form of exposure and current rules.
advantages: Useful for learning diversification across different economic drivers.
Multiple access forms reveal how structure changes cost and liquidity.
limitations: Gold does not generate operating cash flow.
Physical forms introduce purity, storage, and resale considerations.
commonMistakes: Assuming gold always protects purchasing power over every period.

title: Real estate investment trusts
summary: Learn how listed real-estate trusts combine property exposure, market pricing, distributions, and manager risk.
purpose: Studying pooled, listed exposure to income-producing real-estate assets.
riskLabel: Market-linked variability with property, leverage, tenant, and manager risks
variability: Listed prices and distributions can change with rates, occupancy, leverage, and property conditions.
typicalHorizon: Generally studied with a multi-year perspective.
liquidity: Exchange trading can provide access, but price and trading depth can vary.
minimumPracticalAmount: Depends on market price, lot rules, and access channel.
costs: Review management expenses, transaction costs, leverage, and property-level charges.
taxCaveat: Different distribution components can receive different tax treatment.
advantages: Provides a way to study property economics without managing a property directly.
Published reports can make income, occupancy, and leverage more visible.
limitations: Listed pricing can be volatile even when properties are occupied.
Sector or city concentration can be significant.
commonMistakes: Looking only at the distribution rate.
Ignoring leverage, tenant concentration, and asset quality.

title: Direct real estate
summary: Study large-ticket property ownership through affordability, financing, maintenance, concentration, and exit constraints.
purpose: Learning how direct property ownership combines use value, financing, operating costs, and market exposure.
riskLabel: Concentrated, illiquid, and sensitive to location, financing, legal, and property-specific factors
variability: Appraisals can appear stable while achievable sale prices and time-to-exit vary significantly.
liquidity: Low; transactions can take time and involve material friction.
minimumPracticalAmount: Typically substantial, with financing and transaction requirements.
costs: Consider financing, stamp duty, registration, brokerage, maintenance, vacancy, insurance, and repairs.
taxCaveat: Ownership, rental, financing, and transfer can each have separate tax consequences.
advantages: Connects a tangible asset with housing or income objectives.
Makes leverage, cash-flow, and concentration trade-offs concrete.
limitations: A single property can dominate household wealth.
Legal, title, construction, tenant, and maintenance risks require specialist checks.
commonMistakes: Comparing only headline prices and ignoring total ownership cost.
Assuming a quick exit will always be available.
